title.narrative: Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association Core Support
Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association Core Support

description.narrative:
There are three main objectives to this intervention: Objective 1: To strengthen the governance capacity of local level actors to drive sustainability of food security systems, climate resilience and natural resources management.
Objective 2: To strengthen the capacity of communities especially women and young people to influence the design and implementation of climate change and natural resource management policies.
Objective 3: Strengthened institutional capacity of ZELA to contribute to sustainable natural resource governance and climate change resilience.
The intervention should result in poor and marginalised communities in Binga, Gutu and Gwanda becoming more resilient to climate change, improving their sustainable management of natural resources which will enhance their food security and move them towards poverty alleviation. The intervention should also result in the strengthening of ZELA at a time when it is paramount that local CSOs are capacitated and enhanced and are sustainable to meaningfully contribute to the country's development from an environmental lens.

The Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association (ZELA) has been implementing the strengthening community-level governance frameworks for improved food security, climate resilience and environmental sustainability in Binga, Gutu, and Gwanda districts in Zimbabwe intervention through a 26.5 million SEK core support from Sida, October 2021-December 2024. The intervention aims at Strengthening community level governance frameworks for improved food security, climate resilience and environmental sustainability in Zimbabwe by 1) Strengthening institutional capacity of ZELA to contribute to sustainable natural resource governance and climate change resilience. ; 2) To strengthen the governance capacity of local level actors to drive sustainability of food security systems, climate resilience and natural resources management and ; 3) To strengthen the capacity of communities especially women and young people to influence the design and implementation of climate change and natural resource management policies. Through an amendment agreement to the core support with additional activities and funding of 4.5 million SEK, ZELA will continue the work started in 2021 for six months, ending 30 June 2025. The amendment was necessitated by the need to enhance sustainability of the beneficiaries in a changing climatic context as well as incorporating emerging issues such as competing land uses from enhanced critical raw material mining in Zimbabwe. The intervention’s total budget including the 4.5 million SEK added to the agreement amendment is 31 million SEK.

Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association (ZELA) har genom kärnstöd arbetat med att stärka samhällsstyrningen på lokal nivå för ökad livsmedelssäkerhet, stärkt resiliens mot klimateffekter samt varaktigt stärka miljön i Binga, Gutu, Gwanda, and Mbire districts in Zimbabwe från oktober 2021 till december 2024. Projektet syftar till att stärka samhällsstyrningen på lokal nivå för ökad livsmedelssäkerhet, stärkt resiliens mot klimateffekter samt varaktigt stärka miljön i Binga, Gutu, Gwanda, and Mbire districts in Zimbabwe genom att 1) stärka den institutionella kapaciteten hos ZELA för att de skall kunna bidra till uthållig hantering av naturresurser och resiliens mot klimatpåverkan; 2) öka förvaltningskapaciteten hos lokala aktörer för att stärka system för ökad livsmedelsäkerhet, resiliens i klimatfrågor och hantering av naturresurser; 3) stärka lokala samhällens förmåga, särskilt bland kvinnor och ungdomar, att få inflytande över utformning och genomförande av policies för klimatfrågor och hantering av naturresurser. Genom en avtalsändring kommer ZELA att motta ytterligare 4.5 MSEK för att dels fortsätta deras arbete som startade 2021, dels för att lägga till en del aktiviteter med avslut 30 juni 2025. Avtalsändringen var nödvändig för att säkerställa hållbarheten i projektet samt förmågan hos stödmottagarna i en ändrad kontext drabbad av klimatförändringar men också växande problemet med konkurrande markanvändning från gruvsektorn. Insatsens totala budget inklusive avtalsändringen på 4.5 MSK är 31 MSEK.

title.narrative: Decision on Amendment of Contribution - with correct decision number

description.narrative:
This intervention provided core support to the Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association (ZELA), now known as the Zimbabwe Environmental Law Organisation to align with the national mandates under a new law, the Private Voluntary Organisation Act of 2025.
Results Outcome 1: Functional Local-Level Institutions Sustainably Managing Climate Resilience Infrastructure and Natural Resources for Improved Food Security
- Transforming Irrigation Governance into Sustainable Climate-Resilient Institutions The project transformed local-level institutions (mainly irrigation schemes) in Gutu district (Ruti irrigation scheme) and Gwanda district (Silikwe, Bhopoma and Sukwe irrigation scheme), from fragile and conflict-ridden entities into functional, transparent, and productive structures. The sustainability of climate adaptation measures was reinforced through the significant involvement and guidance of local government officials, embedding project outcomes within institutional structures for long-term impact. The irrigation schemes are now anchored on government policy and the law, as it relates to Climate Resilience infrastructure, Food security and broadly environmental sustainability. This makes it easy for the schemes to be recognized as part of the country's agricultural architecture, ensuring continuity beyond project cycles.
- Breaking the Cycle of Water Resource based Conflict: Establishing Governance and Productivity Foundations The project played a pivotal role in defending and securing water tenure rights, particularly for women and young people, who are often the most excluded from decision-making over critical water resources. By promoting and operationalizing the principles of Integrated Water Resource Management (IWRM), the project ensured that water governance shifted toward transparency, equity, and sustainability. Women and youth were not only protected as rights-holders but empowered as active participants in planning, allocation, and oversight of water resources. This strengthened community capacity to manage competing water demands, reduced conflicts, and enhanced climate resilience across districts.
- From Water Resource Conflict to Productivity: Governance Improvements towards food security Productivity improvements significantly strengthened food security and household resilience across the irrigation schemes. At Ruti, farmers recorded harvests of up to 600 kg of beans per farmer, equivalent to USD 540 in gross income, demonstrating how strengthened governance directly translated into increased yields and stable food supplies. These gains were not accidental; they were the outcome of clearer constitutions, equitable water distribution, and transparent leadership systems that eliminated long-standing disputes and improved coordination at plot level.
Such improvements ensured not only higher and more reliable production but also enhanced household nutrition, reduced vulnerability to climate shocks, and strengthened inter-generational well-being. Without these governance reforms, these transformative food security outcomes, including increased surplus production, improved income stability, and greater community cohesion, would not have been possible.
- Governance Gains Driving Food Security, Climate Resilience, and Institutional Accountability By the end of June 2025, farmers now harvested an average of 10 bags of 50kg maize, 30 buckets of beans, and 20 buckets of wheat per season per farmer. Gutu RDC demonstrated leadership by passing an environmental by-law in December 2023, incorporating community recommendations such as stiffer penalties for unsustainable land practices. In Binga district, a communication platform with ZimParks was created, allowing communities to quickly report and address Human-Wildlife Conflicts (HWC), a platform that was absent prior to project commencement.
- Sustainably Managing Climate Resilience Infrastructure and Natural Resources for Improved Food Security Sida-supported infrastructure upgrades at Ruti Irrigation, including pump house construction and electrification, transforming irrigation reliability for 247 farmers in Gutu district, and directly boosting productivity and food security capacity and possibilities for Gutu district farmers. The Sida support not only enhanced governance and infrastructure, but also reduced unsafe night-time irrigation, mitigating gender-based violence risks whilst at the same time increasing yields and empowering women and young farmers.
Farmers under the project, institutionalized sustainability through Savings and Internal Lending Committees (SILCs), pooling resources in Gutu district and Gwanda district, to maintain infrastructure and strengthen financial resilience and governance. The schemes shifted from subsistence to business-oriented enterprises, with 80% of farmers earning an average seasonal income of USD 750 compared to baseline subsistence levels. Improved irrigation functionality attracted significant external investment. Food and Agriculture Organisations (FAOs) support to Silikwe IMC and Governments planned Phase 4 expansion for Ruti irrigation scheme, signal recognition of the schemes as reliable and sustainable institutions.
Outcome 2: Empowered Communities, Especially Women and Youth, Advocate for Inclusive Climate Change and Natural Resource Management (NRM) Policies
- Gender responsive Climate Change and Natural Resource advocacy The project succeeded in promoting inclusive environmental and climate advocacy among target communities in Gutu district and Gwanda district, with regards to women and youth, transforming them from passive observers into active shapers of environmental governance , including climate policy and NRM policies. This shift is important because historically, rural communities have been sidelined in environmental decision-making, with their lived realities rarely informing national policies. By breaking this pattern, the project ensured that climate and natural resource governance in Zimbabwe became more inclusive and responsive, with community voices especially of poor/marginalized women and youth.
- From knowledge acquisition to active participation in decision making Communities in Binga district and Gwanda district, moved from acquiring knowledge to actively engaging in the policy and legal discourse, influencing both local and national decision-making. Women and youth emerged as leaders, environmental conflicts declined, and grassroots voices are now embedded in Zimbabwe's natural resource governance frameworks. This is significant impact, since the project took out communities from a position of being marginalized as voiceless victims of climate change and environmental mismanagement and transformed them into agents of change, capable of shaping laws, influencing policies, and safeguarding their own futures.
- Community voices into policy and legal processes By 20232024, empowerment translated into advocacy capacity and action. Communities directly influenced national policies, submitting inputs into the Parks and Wildlife Amendment Bill and the framework for community conservancies. They called for community ownership of conservancies, fair compensation for HWC losses, streamlined permits, and recognition of Indigenous Knowledge Systems. This was unprecedented: rural voices shaping national legal frameworks that directly affect their livelihoods.
- Community-Led Conservation Gains: Reduced Wildlife Conflict and Rising Youth Environmental Stewardship At the community level, tangible changes emerged in poaching cases dropped from 36 in 2022 to 11 in 2023, while HWC incidents fell from 68 to 38, and problem animals from 8 to 2. Knowledge levels rose further; by December 2024, 91% of communities understood sustainable wildlife management, and 93% understood HWC.
Outcome 3: Strengthened Institutional Capacity of ZELA to contribute to Sustainable Natural Resource Governance and Climate Change Resilience
For objective 3, it is essential to note that the project was under core support. That means that the Sida funding was essentially covering ZELA's strategic areas of need and thus the results that are noted under Objective 3 are linked to ZELA's achievements, successes and impact at organisation level.
- Human rights, democratic governance and accountability (including corruption reduction) Regionally, ZELAs leadership within SADC civil society platforms and participation in African Union policy dialogues elevated community and civil society perspectives on extractives, climate justice, and gender equality in natural resource governance ZELA played a key role in influencing SADC policy positions on critical minerals, corporate accountability, and rights-based ESG standards, aligning them with the African Mining Vision. Internationally, ZELA contributed to the Kimberley Process Civil Society Coalition (KP CSC), advocating for human rightsbased diamond governance and fair benefit sharing in mineral value chains. Its active engagement with the OECD Responsible Business Conduct (RBC) platform positioned ZELA as a Southern voice advancing due diligence, labour rights, and environmental compliance in the mining sector.
The organisation presented at the OECD Responsible Mineral Supply Chain Forum (20232024), showcasing best practices in responsible lithium and gold governance, and co-authored civil society submissions on a just energy transition for UNFCCC COP27 and COP28. ZELA also made technical contributions to the United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA), COP27, and COP28, where it amplified calls for equitable climate financing and the recognition of Environmental, Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights (EESCRs) as integral to climate justice. ZELA also contributed to the African Mining Vision (AMV) and SADC Green Growth dialogues, advancing gender-responsive, climate-aligned governance frameworks across the region.
Sidas support was instrumental in securing ZELAs recognition to participate in the UNFCCC Climate Change Negotiations in Bonn as part of the Government of Zimbabwe delegation, where it provided legal and policy advisory input. Furthermore, ZELAs appointment to the UNFCCC constituted bodies under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement, which governs carbon credit mechanisms, firmly positioned the organisation as a trusted technical actor, aligning Sida-funded initiatives with Zimbabwes obligations under international climate frameworks.
- Strategic Partnerships and Resource Mobilisation The landmark donor conference that was convened in 2024 at Sida, and attracted over 40 strategic partners,including donors and CSOs, led to transformative partnerships with various funding partners. A typical example is the partnership with Hivos, which is envisaged to strengthen ZELOs urban environment programme. ZELA was also throughout the life of the project abe to sure key Memorandum of Understanding with 6 strategic strategic partners including Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority (ZimParks), National Prosecuting Authority, Zimbabwe Republic Police CID Minerals, Flora and Fauna Unit, among others.
- Influence on responsible economic development through strengthened private sector engagement In relation to the mining sector, ZELAs advocacy for Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) compliance and its partnerships with mining stakeholders, including the Chamber of Mines, drove adoption of responsible business practices among at least 10 companies, aligning corporate behaviour with Economic, Environmental, Social and Cultural Rights (EESCRs).
- Robust Institutions for Responsible and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) -Aligned Mining ZELA advanced ESG and environmental safeguards with a base of over 200 artisanal and small-scale miners empowered by ZELA on ESG standards, occupational safety, and responsible sourcing. The organisation commissioned an ESG Scoping Study under the project, focused on critical minerals, specifically lithium, gold, and granite, to strengthen corporate accountability and sustainable mining practices. The study provided a comprehensive analysis of the sectors challenges and opportunities, highlighting persistent issues such as environmental degradation, social inequities, and governance weaknesses, and underscored the urgent need for reform through ethical and sustainable procurement. Key findings emphasized the importance of integrating materiality into ESG frameworks to better address stakeholder needs and enhance transparency in reporting. The study recommended modernising and enforcing regulatory frameworks, building institutional capacity, and fostering multi-stakeholder collaboration among mining companies, government bodies (including the Zimbabwe Investment and Development Agency), civil society, and local communities.
